title: Markdown Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: Markdown Formatting Reference
introduction.description: Markdown is a lightweight syntax for formatting plain text - README files, GitHub comments, issues and PRs, docs sites, and most chat/note apps all render it. Everything below is CommonMark plus the GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) extensions (task lists, tables, strikethrough, footnotes) that GitHub and most modern renderers support.

prerequisites: Any plain text editor - Markdown needs no special tooling to write
A place that renders it, e.g. a GitHub README/PR, VS Code's preview (Ctrl+Shift+V), or a Markdown-aware app

steps.title: Headings
steps.description: Six levels of headings, made by prefixing a line with 1-6 # characters and a space. A single H1 is typically reserved for the page/document title.
steps.note: Leave a blank line before and after a heading - some renderers get it wrong without one.

steps.title: Emphasis
steps.description: Bold, italic, and strikethrough text, plus combinations of the two.
steps.note: Pick one style (* or _) and stick with it in a document - mixing both for the same purpose just makes the raw text harder to scan.

steps.title: Lists
steps.description: Unordered and ordered lists, with nesting via a 2-4 space indent. Ordered list numbers don't actually need to be sequential - Markdown renumbers them for you - but sequential is easier to read in the source.
steps.note: A list item followed by a blank line and then 4-space-indented text keeps that text inside the same item, e.g. for a longer explanation under a bullet.

steps.title: Task Lists
steps.description: GitHub Flavored Markdown extension: checkboxes inside a list, checked with an x. Renders as interactive checkboxes on GitHub (clickable if you have write access to the file).
steps.note: The space inside the brackets matters - [ ] is unchecked, [x] is checked, [X] also works.

steps.title: Links & Images
steps.description: Inline links, optional-title links, reusable reference-style links, bare-URL autolinks, and images - which use the exact same syntax as a link with a ! in front.
steps.note: Image alt text isn't just decoration - it's what screen readers announce and what shows if the image fails to load, so keep it descriptive.

steps.title: Code
steps.description: Inline code with single backticks for short snippets, and fenced code blocks (triple backticks) for anything longer. Add a language name right after the opening fence to get syntax highlighting.
steps.note: Need a literal backtick inside inline code? Wrap it in double backticks instead: `` `backtick` ``.

steps.title: Blockquotes
steps.description: Quoted text, prefixed with >. Consecutive > lines join into one quoted paragraph; a blank >  line separates paragraphs within the quote, and quotes can nest or contain other Markdown.
steps.note: Blockquotes are commonly (mis)used for callout boxes - GFM alerts (see the Extras step) are the purpose-built version of that.

steps.title: Tables
steps.description: GFM tables: a header row, a separator row of dashes, then data rows, all pipe-delimited. Colons in the separator row set column alignment (left, center, right).
steps.note: Pipes don't need to line up visually in the source - renderers only care about the pipe characters, not the whitespace around them.

steps.title: Horizontal Rules & Line Breaks
steps.description:
A horizontal rule (---, ***, or ___ on its own line) draws a divider. Markdown normally collapses single newlines into spaces within a paragraph - forcing a line break needs two trailing spaces or an explicit
.
steps.note:
Trailing spaces are invisible and easy to lose (e.g. to an editor's trim-on-save setting) -
is more explicit and safer to rely on.

steps.title: Extras (GFM)
steps.description: A few more GitHub Flavored Markdown extensions: footnotes, a collapsible <details> section (raw HTML, which Markdown always allows inline), escaping characters that would otherwise trigger formatting, and GFM alert callouts (NOTE, TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION).
steps.note: Alert callouts (> [!NOTE] etc.) are GitHub-specific - they render as plain blockquotes on renderers that don't support them, so they degrade gracefully.
